summary: Introduces Dual-Stack Lite, which helps broadband providers share IPv4 addresses among customers while rolling out IPv6. It combines two familiar techniques, tunneling IPv4 inside IPv6 and network address translation, to better balance the costs and benefits of IPv6 deployment.

plainLanguage.summary: Dual-Stack Lite lets a provider carry customers' IPv4 traffic across an IPv6 network. A provider-side router removes the IPv6 tunnel and shares IPv4 addresses among customers.

subtitle: A way to carry customers' IPv4 traffic across an IPv6 provider network and share IPv4 addresses.

tldr.problem: The free pool of IPv4 addresses was depleted before IPv6 deployment was sufficient. Providers still need to support IPv4 services with limited address space.
tldr.mechanism: Dual-Stack Lite tunnels IPv4 packets inside IPv6 from a B4 function to an AFTR. The AFTR decapsulates the packets and uses IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT to share addresses among customers.
tldr.outcome: Providers can use IPv6 in their access network while customers continue to use IPv4 services. RFC 6333 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 7335.

today: RFC 6333 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7335. It has not been obsoleted according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Dual-Stack Lite Was Defined
sections.content:
RFC 6333 introduces Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) for providers that need to keep offering IPv4 services while deploying IPv6. It combines IPv4-in-IPv6 tunneling with Network Address Translation (NAT) to let customers share IPv4 addresses.

The document distinguishes dual-stack-capable devices, which implement both IP versions, from dual-stack-provisioned devices, which have both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses configured. Pure IPv6-only devices are outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers can deploy IPv6 before all customers and services have left IPv4. DS-Lite carries IPv4 traffic through the provider's IPv6 network.

sections.title: The Tunnel from Customer to Provider
sections.content:
Instead of placing multiple NATs in a row, DS-Lite sends IPv4 packets through an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel to a carrier-grade NAT in the provider network. The tunnel can end at different points in that network, and customers' overlapping private IPv4 address spaces can be distinguished by their tunnel endpoints.

Communication stays within one IP address family: IPv4 hosts communicate with IPv4 destinations, and IPv6 hosts with IPv6 destinations. The system does not translate between IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 packets travel inside IPv6 packets to a NAT in the provider network. IPv6 traffic follows normal IPv6 routing and does not use this tunnel.

sections.title: The B4 Element at the Customer Side
sections.content:
The B4 is a function on a customer device or gateway that creates a tunnel to an AFTR. The RFC defines an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel. A home gateway should not run another NAT between the home network and the B4, to avoid double NAT.

The tunnel adds IPv6 header space and reduces the effective MTU. The provider can increase link MTUs between the B4 and AFTR by at least 40 bytes. If that is not possible, the B4 must fragment after IPv6 encapsulation and reassemble before decapsulation; it must not fragment the inner IPv4 packet.

The B4 needs the AFTR's IPv6 address, which can be configured manually or obtained through DHCPv6. The RFC recommends that B4 implementations support the DHCPv6 option in RFC 6334. It also recommends a DNS proxy for IPv4 hosts when the B4 receives DNS server information over IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The B4 wraps each IPv4 packet in IPv6 and sends it to the AFTR. It also needs a way to find the AFTR and provide DNS service to IPv4 hosts.

sections.title: The AFTR and Its Extended Binding Table
sections.content:
The AFTR combines an IPv4-in-IPv6 tunnel endpoint with IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT. It removes the IPv6 tunnel, translates the IPv4 packet and sends it toward the IPv4 destination. Return traffic is translated back and tunneled to the correct B4.

The AFTR extends its NAT binding table with the source IPv6 address of incoming packets. This lets it distinguish customers who use overlapping private IPv4 addresses and reconstruct the right IPv6 tunnel for replies without static per-tunnel configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: The AFTR removes the tunnel and translates IPv4 packets. It records the source IPv6 address with each NAT binding so replies return to the right customer.

sections.title: NAT Behavior and Service Limits
sections.content:
An AFTR must follow the NAT behavior requirements in RFC 4787, RFC 5508 and RFC 5382. An operator may configure separate NAT pools, but their address ranges must not overlap.

Because the AFTR performs NAT, some applications may need an application-level gateway; the RFC names Active FTP as an example. The shared device cannot implement every current or future gateway. Shared IPv4 addresses also raise logging and port-allocation issues. The RFC points to Port Control Protocol work for applications that need port forwarding or longer mapping lifetimes.
sections.plainLanguage: DS-Lite inherits the limits of NAT. Some applications may need extra support, and the provider must manage shared addresses, ports and customer records.

sections.title: Source Checks and Logging
sections.content:
When the AFTR decapsulates a packet, it MUST forward only packets sourced from RFC 1918 addresses, the reserved DS-Lite range or other addresses authorized out of band. It must drop other packets to prevent devices from sending unauthorized source addresses through the provider network.

Since an IPv4 address and timestamp no longer identify one customer, the AFTR should be able to log the tunnel identifier, protocol, ports, addresses and creation time of each NAT binding. The RFC also recommends limits on per-user port use and ways to restrict service to registered customers.
sections.plainLanguage: The AFTR checks packet sources before forwarding them. Because customers share addresses, the provider needs binding records that identify the tunnel and connection details.
